raw_response:
Seven useful precedents cover distinct byte literals, individual byte values, and alternative ways to build mixed binary data.

1. **[Python 3.3.5 bytes literals](https://docs.python.org/release/3.3.5/reference/lexical_analysis.html).** A b-prefixed literal combines readable ASCII with escaped arbitrary bytes while remaining separate from Unicode text. This directly informs byte-sequence spelling and type separation. A single-byte literal still denotes a sequence; [indexing returns an integer](https://docs.python.org/release/3.3.5/library/stdtypes.html), whereas slicing preserves the bytes type. Both opened snapshots were last updated March 9, 2014.

2. **[Racket 5.3.6 byte strings](https://download.racket-lang.org/docs/5.3.6/html/guide/bytestrings.html).** Its # prefix distinguishes byte strings, retaining readable ASCII and escaped binary values; byte output performs no character encoding. Individual bytes are integers from 0 to 255, and conversion to characters explicitly selects an encoding. The [official release table](https://download.racket-lang.org/all-versions.html) dates 5.3.6 to August 2013.

3. **[OCaml 4.01 characters and strings](https://caml.inria.fr/distrib/ocaml-4.01/ocaml-4.01-refman.html).** Single quotes express one 8-bit character, double quotes express sequences, and both share numeric escapes. This supplies a consistent individual-byte and sequence notation. Its upper bytes have Latin-1 character semantics; adapting the spelling should preserve Rust's existing Unicode types. The manual is dated September 12, 2013.

4. **[Go strings as byte sequences](https://go.dev/blog/strings).** Strings can contain arbitrary bytes, with readable source fragments, hexadecimal escapes, and byte indexing even for invalid UTF-8. This is useful for preserving mixed content and inspecting individual bytes. Unescaped non-ASCII source text is UTF-8, and range loops decode runes, so those operations must remain distinct. The official explanation is dated October 23, 2013.

5. **[Erlang bit syntax](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/bit_syntax.html).** Binary construction and matching combine readable string segments, numeric bytes, and explicitly sized fields. This offers a compositional alternative for protocol or document fragments. It is more extensive than literal syntax alone: alignment, field size, and endianness matter. Date status is unknown because only live OTP 29.1.2 documentation was verified.

6. **[Haskell Data.ByteString.Char8](https://downloads.haskell.org/~ghc/7.6.3/docs/html/libraries/bytestring-0.10.0.2/Data-ByteString-Char8.html).** The pack and singleton functions, plus overloaded string literals, offer a library-based way to turn readable notation into byte storage. The key caveat is truncation to eight bits, which can lose information for unrestricted Unicode input. The historical version was opened, but its publication date was not independently verified.

7. **[D hexadecimal strings and byte escapes](https://dlang.org/spec/lex.html).** Numeric byte escapes support mixed readable and binary content, while hexadecimal strings represent dense binary sequences that need not be valid UTF. The alternative hex form sacrifices ASCII readability, and ordinary source characters retain Unicode encoding behavior. Date status is unknown for the opened live specification.
